points.description: States that removing electrons reduces electron–electron repulsion (fewer electrons remaining, so remaining electrons are held more tightly).
Links the reduced electron–electron repulsion to lower (more negative) potential energy of the remaining electrons.
States that the 3rd and 4th electrons removed feel the same core charge (equal effective nuclear charge, e.g. +4 for the n=3 electrons).
States that the 3rd and 4th electrons are both removed from the n=3 shell and so have the same (similar) radius.
States that the 5th electron is removed from the n=2 shell (inner shell) and feels a higher core charge (e.g. +10 minus 2 other n=2 electrons... greater than that of n=3 electrons).
States that the 5th electron, in the n=2 shell, is at a much smaller radius (closer to the nucleus).

Correctly relates potential energy to ionization energy using Coulomb's law (V ∝ −Q₁Q₂/r): lower (more negative) potential energy, from higher core charge and/or smaller radius, means more energy is needed to remove the electron. Use this to explain that IE3 and IE4 are similar-ish (modest increase from reduced repulsion) while IE5 is a much larger jump.
points.partial_credit: 1 mark if Coulomb's law relationship to ionization energy is stated correctly but not applied to explain the relative magnitudes (or vice versa).

rubric.notes: Full marks need each listed idea; equivalent wording accepted. Core charge numbers need not match exactly if the reasoning (same for 3rd/4th, higher for 5th) is correct. No marks for merely restating that the values increase.
